newsitem.title: USA: New York judge bars sale of European oil painting.
newsitem.headline: New York judge bars sale of European oil painting.

text.p: A judge on Thursday barred a New York college professor from selling an oil painting that a Polish prince said the Nazis stole from his family during the Second World War.

Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Emily Goodman said she wanted the lawyer for Prince Adam Karol Czartoryski-Borbon of Poland to clarify whether the German government or a German reparations committee ought to be part of the case.

The painting was put up for sale by Donald Turcotte, an Ithaca, New York, geophysicist who is a professor at Cornell University. He consigned the painting to Sotheby's auction gallery for a January 1997 sale. Sotheby's put an asking price on it of between $70,000 and $90,000.
The auction house was holding the painting while it waited for a resolution to the dispute between Turcotte and Czartoryski. Sotheby's had no legal involvement.
The oil painting, by Dutch master Jan Mostaert, is known as "Portrait of a Lady, presumably Anne of Bretagne."
After Czartoryski became aware of the pending sale, Sotheby's was sent papers claiming proof of ownership of the work, his lawyer said.

In papers filed in Manhattan Supreme Court on May 2, Czartoryski said that at the time of the 1939 Nazi invasion of Poland, the painting was in the Goluchow collection belonging to his family. He said that when his uncle died in 1978, he inherited the estate, including the painting.
Czartoryski, 57, a business consultant, lives in London. He is a cousin of Juan Carlos, the King of Spain.

"The painting has been in my family over 200 years," the prince said in a telephone news conference at his lawyer's office. "All I know is that it was confiscated in January 1942 by the Nazis and held in the National Museum in Warsaw until it disappeared from circulation."

In the Provenance, Sotheby's lists the Archbishop of Salzburg in Austria as the owner of the painting after the prince's family. But how the painting turned up in a collection owned by the Archbishop, remained a mystery.
The painting next surfaced when the M. Knoeder and Co. gallery in New York sold it to Turcotte's mother in 1958. She gave it to her son in 1963, court papers said.
